title: Learning ground state observables from quantum computing experiments
authors: Ben Jaderberg, Freya Shah, Minjun Jeon, M. Emre Sahin, Christa Zoufal, Kunal Sharma
abstract: Recent theoretical progress has established conditions under which machine learning models can efficiently predict ground-state properties of gapped local Hamiltonians when trained on quantum-generated data. Previous experimental demonstrations in this paradigm, however, have largely been limited to small systems or highly structured states, due to the difficulty of preparing many-body ground states on quantum processors. In this work, we demonstrate learning from experimental quantum data generated from approximate ground states of the two-dimensional Heisenberg XXZ model with system sizes up to 115 qubits. We construct a dataset of single-site expectation values, two-point correlations, and 12-body loop correlations across the antiferromagnetic phase. We then train neural networks on this data and show that they can accurately predict spatially resolved observables for previously unseen Hamiltonian parameters, both within the training distribution and in an out-of-distribution regime approaching the phase boundary. Our results demonstrate the practical realization of learning from quantum data for an interacting two-dimensional many-body system at scale, motivating a path toward regimes where quantum processors could provide training data beyond the reach of classical approximation methods.
summary: The paper presents an end-to-end methodology for extracting physical knowledge from experimental quantum computation results. By applying SKQD and variational optimization to generate ground state data for the 2D XXZ model, they train advanced neural networks to predict complex observables. This demonstrates a powerful paradigm shift: using near-term quantum hardware not just for simulation, but as a scalable source of training data for predictive physics models.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a workflow to learn ground-state observables of interacting quantum many-body systems directly from data generated by near-term quantum computing experiments.
main_result: The authors successfully trained machine learning models on quantum data for the 2D Heisenberg XXZ model, demonstrating accurate prediction of local observables even in out-of-distribution regimes approaching a phase boundary.
method: A combined approach uses Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (SKQD) to generate approximate ground states, followed by training sophisticated neural networks (comparing global vs. geometry-aware architectures) on the resulting expectation values.
model_or_system: The system studied is the spin-1/2 XXZ model on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, parameterized by the anisotropy $J_z$. The study focuses on the antiferromagnetic phase and its approach to quantum critical points.
key_observables: Single-site expectation values ($\langle Z angle$), two-point correlations ($C_{zz}$), 12-body loop correlations ($\langle Z_{	ext{loop}} angle$), and the staggered magnetization ($m_s$).
important_parameters: System sizes up to $n=115$ qubits; anisotropy parameter $J_z$; training regimes span from $1.6 \le J_z \le 6.0$, with testing near $J_z = 1.0$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve the feasibility of SKQD generating sufficiently accurate data, and that ML architectures (especially geometry-aware ones) can capture complex spatial correlations beyond simple parameter dependence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow overview, energy error convergence relative to DMRG across $J_z$, and comparative plots showing the mean relative error ($\Delta O_{ML}$) of observables predicted by different ML architectures when extrapolating towards phase boundaries.
paper_structure: The paper details a multi-step process: first, generating data using SKQD combined with variational basis optimization to improve ground state estimates; second, designing and training two distinct neural network architectures (global vs. local/geometry-aware) on this quantum data; and finally, rigorously testing the models' generalization capability both within and outside the trained parameter regime.
why_interesting: This work bridges theoretical condensed matter physics with practical quantum machine learning, showing a concrete path to using noisy, limited quantum hardware outputs as high-fidelity training data for complex many-body simulations that are otherwise computationally intractable or too resource-intensive classically.
